Keywords: remote add origin upstream fork URL configure push pull
Description: Add a named remote to the repository. origin is the convention for your primary remote. upstream is used for the original repo when working with forks.
When to Use: Connecting a local repo to GitHub/GitLab, or adding the upstream for a fork
Command Example:
# Add origin
git remote add origin https://github.com/leodyversemilla07/multichain-explorer-2.git

# Add upstream for a fork
git remote add upstream https://github.com/original-owner/repo.git

# List remotes
git remote -v

# Remove a remote
git remote remove old-remote
Gotchas: A remote is just a name and URL — it doesn't pull or push automatically. After adding a remote you still need git fetch or git push.

Keywords: push origin branch -u upstream force set-upstream tracking
Description: Push local commits to a remote. Use -u on first push to set tracking. Use --force-with-lease instead of --force to avoid clobbering others' work.
When to Use: After committing locally and wanting to share or back up your branch
Command Example:
# First push: set tracking
git push -u origin feature/add-cors-middleware

# Subsequent pushes (tracking set)
git push

# Safer force push (fails if remote changed since your last fetch)
git push --force-with-lease

# Delete a remote branch
git push origin --delete old-feature-branch
Gotchas: Never use git push --force on shared branches (main/develop). --force-with-lease is always safer. Force push rewrites remote history and strands collaborators.

Keywords: fetch pull remote update local merge rebase download
Description: git fetch downloads remote changes without applying them. git pull fetches then merges (or rebases). Use fetch to inspect before merging.
When to Use: Use fetch to review what changed on the remote before merging. Use pull when ready to integrate
Command Example:
# Fetch all remotes without merging
git fetch --all

# Fetch and prune stale remote refs
git fetch --prune

# Pull with rebase instead of merge
git pull --rebase

# Check what will be pulled before merging
git fetch origin
git log HEAD..origin/main --oneline
Gotchas: git pull --rebase can cause conflicts just like regular rebase. Set pull.rebase=true in git config to always rebase instead of merge on pull.

Keywords: clone shallow depth partial sparse filter large repo
Description: Clone a remote repository. Use --depth for shallow clone (faster). Use --filter=blob:none for blobless clone of large repos.
When to Use: Starting work on an existing project or creating a local copy of a remote
Command Example:
# Standard clone
git clone https://github.com/leodyversemilla07/multichain-explorer-2.git

# Shallow clone (last 1 commit — fastest CI usage)
git clone --depth=1 https://github.com/owner/repo.git

# Clone and immediately checkout a branch
git clone -b develop https://github.com/owner/repo.git

# Blobless clone (all history but no blobs — good balance)
git clone --filter=blob:none https://github.com/owner/repo.git
Gotchas: Shallow clones break some Git operations like git bisect and full blame. For development always use a full clone. Use shallow only in CI.

Keywords: fork upstream sync update behind ahead diverged rebase merge
Description: Keep your fork in sync with the original repository's main branch. Fetch upstream changes then merge or rebase your fork's main onto them.
When to Use: Before starting new work on a fork, or when a PR shows 'this branch is behind upstream'
Command Example:
# Add upstream once
git remote add upstream https://github.com/original/repo.git

# Sync your fork's main with upstream
git fetch upstream
git switch main
git rebase upstream/main

# Push the updated main to your fork
git push origin main --force-with-lease
Gotchas: If your fork's main has diverged (you committed directly to it) rebase may conflict. Keep fork's main clean — only push to feature branches.

Keywords: tag push remote annotated lightweight release version
Description: Push tags to the remote. Tags are NOT pushed automatically with git push — they must be pushed explicitly.
When to Use: After creating a release tag, to publish it to GitHub so the release appears
Command Example:
# Push a single tag
git push origin v2.0.0

# Push all local tags
git push origin --tags

# Create an annotated tag and push
git tag -a v2.0.0 -m 'Release v2.0.0: adds CORS and exception guard'
git push origin v2.0.0

# Delete a remote tag
git push origin --delete v1.9.0-rc
Gotchas: git push --tags pushes ALL tags including old or draft ones. Push specific tags individually for better control. Use annotated tags (-a) for releases.

Keywords: remote set-url change update https ssh url migrate
Description: Change the URL of an existing remote — useful when switching from HTTPS to SSH or when a repository is moved.
When to Use: Switching authentication method from HTTPS to SSH, or after a repo rename on GitHub
Command Example:
# Change from HTTPS to SSH
git remote set-url origin git@github.com:leodyversemilla07/multichain-explorer-2.git

# Verify the change
git remote -v

# Add a push-only URL (different from fetch URL)
git remote set-url --push origin git@github.com:leodyversemilla07/backup.git
Gotchas: After changing to SSH ensure your SSH key is configured in GitHub Settings > SSH Keys. Test with ssh -T git@github.com before pushing.

Keywords: sparse checkout partial clone large monorepo subdirectory only
Description: Check out only a specific subdirectory of a large repository rather than the entire working tree. Useful for monorepos.
When to Use: Working in a large monorepo where you only need a specific service or package
Command Example:
# Enable sparse checkout
git clone --no-checkout https://github.com/owner/monorepo.git
cd monorepo
git sparse-checkout init --cone
git sparse-checkout set services/auth services/api
git checkout main
Gotchas: Sparse checkout complicates cross-service refactoring since you can't see other directories. Use only for read-heavy / CI scenarios.
